turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files describing perovskite solar cells as
complete devices — `substrate` (glass + transparent electrode), `etl`
(electron-transport layer stack), `htl` (hole-transport layer stack),
`backcontact` (metal / carbon back electrode), `deposition` (absorber
deposition procedure; `>>` separates steps). Every candidate below uses the
same MAPbI3 absorber in the same n-i-p (regular) architecture; they differ
only in the remaining columns. Each row is a device CONFIGURATION whose
efficiency is the median over at least 3 independently fabricated cells, so
it is a reproducible recipe rather than a single champion cell:
  - b3_pvk_stack_train.csv: 300 configurations with the measured power
    conversion efficiency (%).
  - b3_pvk_stack_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE configurations whose power
    conversion efficiency (%) was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same device columns.

Using the training data, select the 5 candidates with the HIGHEST power
conversion efficiency (%).

Reason from the device physics — band alignment and selectivity of the
transport layers, interface recombination, contact chemistry and the film
quality the process is likely to give — then end your answer with an
explicit ranked list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902,
c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
My predicted top five are **c064, c005, c017, c043, and c083**. I prioritize close high-performing training analogues, then interfaces likely to suppress recombination without sacrificing charge extraction. These are predictions of configuration-level median efficiency—not measured candidate efficiencies.

| Rank | Candidate | Training evidence and device-physics rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **c064** | **TiO2-c / SnO2-np / Spiro-MeOTAD / Au.** The same ETL stack appears in the highest-efficiency training configuration, **20.85%**, although with Ag and an additional dip-coating step. Another TiO2-c / SnO2 device reaches **17.47%**. Compact TiO2 provides electrode coverage and hole blocking; the SnO2 overlayer offers favorable electron extraction and can improve the absorber-facing interface. Spiro-MeOTAD/Au provides a well-established selective hole contact. I would not transfer the 20.85% result directly because the absorber process differs. |
| **2** | **c005** | **TiO2-c / PCBM-60 / PCDTBT8 / MoO3 / Au.** Its closest training analogue, using FTO and PCDTBT1, reaches **19.35%** with the same two-step absorber-deposition sequence. PCBM can passivate oxide/perovskite interfacial traps while retaining electron selectivity; the polymer HTL and MoO3/Au contact offer a plausible low-loss hole-extraction pathway. The principal uncertainty is that PCDTBT8 need not reproduce PCDTBT1’s energetics, mobility, or film morphology. |
| **3** | **c017** | **Modified C60 / doped TaTm / Ag, co-evaporated absorber.** Apart from capitalization differences in the material labels, this closely matches the **17.9%** training device with Au. Fullerene electron selectivity and F6-TCNNQ-doped hole transport support low recombination and low series resistance. Co-evaporation can give continuous, controlled absorber films. Ag introduces contact-chemistry uncertainty, but the underlying selective-contact design has unusually direct training support. |
| **4** | **c043** | **Mesoporous TiO2 / DAHI / Spiro-MeOTAD / Au.** This retains the established electron-extraction scaffold and adds an absorber/HTL interfacial modifier. Relevant training configurations reach **18.01%** with PMMA/Spiro-MeOTAD and **16.15%** with graphene oxide/Spiro-MeOTAD. A sufficiently thin, compatible DAHI treatment could reduce surface traps and nonradiative recombination while preserving hole extraction. Its benefit is an extrapolation, not directly measured in the training set. |
| **5** | **c083** | **TiO2-c / dimethylbiguanide / Spiro-MeOTAD / Au.** The nitrogen-rich modifier provides a plausible route to coordinating undercoordinated interfacial ions and modifying the interface dipole. Related interface-engineered training devices reach **17.37–17.405%** with acid modifiers or graphene quantum dots. This candidate has credible voltage and fill-factor upside, although coverage, thickness, and chemical compatibility are important unknowns. |

**Confidence is higher for the first three.** The last two depend more strongly on successful molecular passivation; the supplied labels do not specify the thicknesses, processing conditions, or energetics needed to guarantee that benefit.

Final: c064, c005, c017, c043, c083
